prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and its development to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B034 to B013, with Katori and Ye only. The reason is that the chair asked whether I can state a B034 priority statement that survives the Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam, Mead-Truhlar, Herzberg-Longuet-Higgins, Simon and Bohm objections, and after the exchange I cannot do so with the confidence a final public position needs. Berry's 1984 paper is a clean statement of the adiabatic geometric phase, but a citation honouring 'discovery' must say who discovered what, and the Aharonov-Bohm half of the pair has a deceased co-author and an earlier claim. I would be putting forward a candidate whose credit I could not defend, which is the very standard I applied to others in round 1. B013 is the better answer to my own test of what the essential mechanism is and who first identified it. The mechanism is simple and checkable: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift is the same for both clock levels, and the atoms are confined without perturbing the transition, while thousands of atoms are interrogated at once. Katori identified that mechanism and built the first strontium lattice clocks; Ye's group carried it to the 10^-18 level and developed the many-body clock. The result was then reproduced at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, which is the experimental contact and independent confirmation I value. The clock now also serves as a many-body quantum system and a probe of gravitational redshift across millimetres, so it is more than an incremental record. On the chair's first question, I would word the citation around the lattice concept and the many-atom regime that ion clocks cannot reach, and not around clocks or combs in general, so it does not read as a third clock prize.
statement.case_against: I do not drop the earlier reservation. The frequency-comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes cover much of the lineage, and a sceptic can call the lattice clock a very successful refinement and not a new phenomenon. No varying-constant or dark-sector signal has come out of the clocks yet, and the redefinition of the second is still pending. The two-name credit leaves out Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, Lemonde, Campbell and Hollberg, and I cannot weigh their roles from the files. These are real costs, but I judge them less severe than the unresolved credit and priority problems of B034, and the lattice concept is a separate, well-defined invention. I also note that my move came after seeing how others reasoned, so I should say that I am convinced by the attribution and reproducibility arguments and not by the count of supporters.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct concept with a many-atom statistical gain that ion clocks cannot offer, that the citation should be worded around the lattice concept, and that a Nobel Prize recognises demonstrated performance and not the metrological decision on the second.
responses.response: In round 1 I said I did not know whether this marked a completed discovery or an engineering trajectory. Kroll's argument answers most of that for me. The statistical gain of many atoms with Stark and motional shifts controlled is a mechanism, not just a record, and the redefinition of the second is a political and metrological decision the prize need not wait for. I accept the wording safeguard and have written my citation around magic-wavelength trapping. I still think a varying-constant or dark-sector result would make the case far stronger, but that is a reason to value the instrument, not to postpone it.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B048 first as a new state of matter, but concedes that the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit, the 3D topological insulator work and the 2016 prize make attribution fragile, and names B013 as the safer fallback.
responses.response: I made the case in round 1 that B048 builds on Berry curvature and Z2 invariants, and I still believe it. Eriksson's own account of the problem is the reason I do not follow him. Zhang is deceased, the HgTe proposal was decisive, and a three-name cap cannot cover both the 2D and 3D work. I cannot offer a three-person B048 citation that survives those objections, so I will not push it as the final position. I keep B048 as a ballot alternative because the physics is sound and new, and I would revisit it if the committee found a framing around the 2D quantum spin Hall effect that is fair to the people who made it possible.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B013 but concedes it may read as superb metrology and that she cannot reliably weigh Ye's group colleagues, Lemonde, Takamoto and Hollberg from memory. She lists B034 as a third alternative.
responses.response: I share her uncertainty about the wider credit, and I do not think either of us can settle it from recollection. I disagree with the framing that this is only metrology. A lattice with a magic wavelength turns a set of atoms into a controlled many-body system whose systematic shifts are understood at the 10^-18 level, and that is a statement about the physics of the atom-light system, not just an engineering result. On her B034 alternative I agree that it deserves to stay on the list, but I now see that the Bohm problem and the priority claims need a body of historical work we do not have in front of us.

responses.point: Pearce, as Chair, supports B013 for Katori and Ye with distinct, complementary roles, but is not an atomic physicist and wants expert reviewer input on the relative priority of Katori, Ye and earlier lattice-clock proposals.
responses.response: I agree that an expert check on early lattice-clock priority would be sensible, and I would support one before the ballot. I am not an atomic physicist either, so I cannot supply it. From my reading, Katori's proposal and first Sr lattice clocks predate the 10^-18 evaluations, and Ye's JILA programme took the accuracy and many-body work further. That gives two well-separated roles, which is what I could not offer for B034. I would ask the committee to treat the expert review as a check on the two-name attribution and not as a reason to delay.

uncertainties: Whether the two-name Katori and Ye attribution survives an expert review of Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, Lemonde, Campbell and Hollberg, and of the early lattice-clock proposals.
Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on the citation wording.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second, or the absence of a delivered fundamental-physics result, should delay the prize.
My knowledge of atomic physics is second-hand, and I rely on recollection and not verified documents for the priority history of both B013 and B034.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I am in the Gothenburg physics environment close to Chalmers colleagues, but I have no collaboration or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited person on the shortlist, and my frequent co-authors are in turbulence, aerosol and population-genetics work. I do not request recusal.
